name: Book Review Platform
tagline: Reviews save instantly, and a BullMQ worker adds AI summaries, sentiment and tags in the background.
summary: A full-stack book review platform where reviews save instantly while AI enrichment happens asynchronously, so the user never waits on a model call.

Reviews are queued through BullMQ on Redis and picked up by a separate worker process that generates a concise summary, sentiment, and relevant tags with Mastra AI. Cover images live in S3-compatible object storage, and the whole stack runs containerized behind Nginx.

caseStudy.headline: The review saves now. The AI catches up later.
problem: Put a model call inside the request and every review becomes as slow, and as fragile, as the AI provider. A timeout would mean a lost review.
So the review and its enrichment are split: the write is synchronous and cheap, and the AI work is a background job that can be slow, retried, or fail without touching what the user wrote.

stackGroups.label: frontend
stackGroups.items: Next.js App Router · React · TypeScript · Tailwind

stackGroups.label: ops
stackGroups.items: Docker Compose · Nginx · GitHub Actions · RustFS (S3)

flow.title: Lifecycle of a review
flow.failState: failed, but the review is kept
steps: User submits a review. The API validates it and saves it with ai_enrichment_status = pending.
The API enqueues a BullMQ job and returns 201 immediately.
The frontend polls briefly and shows the pending AI state on the review card.
The worker picks up the job, marks the review processing, and calls Mastra AI.
The worker stores summary, sentiment_score and tags, then marks the review completed.
The review card updates in place when enrichment finishes.

decisions.title: The write never waits on AI
decisions.body: The review is saved before any job exists, so a slow or failing model can never cost the user their content.

decisions.title: Jobs live outside the API
decisions.body: A dedicated backend-worker process consumes the queue, isolating background work from request handling.

decisions.title: Enqueue failure is a state
decisions.body: If Redis enqueueing fails after the save, the review is kept and marked with a failed AI state instead of disappearing.

deploy.comment: local, with Compose Watch syncing source changes
production, using prebuilt images from Docker Hub

name: AI-Powered Notes with RAG
tagline: Create notes, then ask questions about them through retrieval-augmented generation with OpenAI, with real-time sync on Convex.
summary: Note AI is an intelligent note-taking application powered by AI, with real-time sync backed by Convex.
It lets users create and manage notes, then ask questions about them using retrieval-augmented generation with OpenAI.

caseStudy.headline: Ask your notes, not the internet.
problem: Notes pile up faster than anyone rereads them, and keyword search only finds what you remember wording exactly.

Note AI embeds every note the moment it's saved, so you can ask a question in plain language and get an answer from your own notes. Each answer links back to the notes it came from, and when nothing matches it simply says it can't find that.

stackGroups.label: frontend
stackGroups.items: Next.js 15 · React 19 · Tailwind v4 · Radix UI

stackGroups.label: ai
stackGroups.items: Vercel AI SDK v5 · gpt-4.1-mini · text-embedding-3-small

flow.title: Answering a question
flow.failState: no match, so it says "can't find that in your notes"
steps: The chat posts to a Convex HTTP route with the user's auth token, and gets a 401 without one. Only the last 10 messages go to the model.
gpt-4.1-mini decides whether it needs the notes and calls the findRelatedNotes tool with a search query.
The query is embedded with text-embedding-3-small and run against the noteEmbeddings vector index, filtered to that user.
Matches scoring 0.3 or lower are dropped. The rest are turned back into whole notes, with duplicates removed.
The model answers from those notes in markdown, linking each source as /notes?noteId=…, and the reply streams into the chat.

decisions.title: Embed meaning, not the whole note
decisions.body: A note is split on blank lines and every paragraph gets its own embedding, so a question can land on the one paragraph that answers it.

decisions.title: The model decides when to search
decisions.body: Retrieval is exposed as a tool instead of being stuffed into every prompt, so small talk costs no vector search and answers cite real note ids.

decisions.title: Users can't retrieve each other's notes
decisions.body: The vector index filters on userId inside the search itself, rather than trusting a filter applied after results come back.

decisions.title: A note never exists without its vectors
decisions.body: The note and its embeddings are inserted in a single Convex mutation, and deleting a note removes its embeddings with it.

name: bunship
tagline: Scaffolds production-ready Bun monorepos using each framework's official scaffolder.
summary: A CLI that scaffolds production-ready Bun monorepos by orchestrating each framework's official scaffolder non-interactively, so generated code always matches upstream instead of drifting from a hand-maintained template.

On top of that it layers an opinionated root toolchain: Bun workspaces, oxlint and oxfmt, knip for dead-code detection, husky pre-commit hooks, and optional Docker plus GitHub Actions VPS deployment. Published to npm as create-bunship.

caseStudy.headline: Upstream writes the app. bunship wires everything around it.
problem: Every new project starts the same way. You run a framework scaffolder, then spend an afternoon wiring up the monorepo around it: workspaces, linting, formatting, dead-code checks, git hooks, Docker and CI.

Hand-maintained templates fix that once, then fall behind the moment a framework ships a new major version. bunship leaves the app code to each framework's official scaffolder and only owns the layer around it. Every generated repo has to pass its own bun run check and bun run build from the very first commit.

stackGroups.label: cli
stackGroups.items: TypeScript · runs on Node ≥ 20 · zero runtime deps (tsdown bundle)

stackGroups.label: generated repo
stackGroups.items: Bun workspaces · oxlint · oxfmt · knip · husky

flow.title: The pipeline of a run
flow.failState: step fails → exit 1, manifest names the step
steps: preflight checks the Node version each selected framework needs and fails fast with the version it found.
Each adapter runs its official scaffolder non-interactively, then patches its app into the workspace: package name, ports, a /health endpoint on APIs.
agentSkills installs framework playbooks first, so tooling can describe what actually landed rather than what was planned.
tooling merges every adapter's fragments into one set of root configs: oxlint, oxfmt, knip, gitignore, AGENTS.md.
docker and cicd add prod and hot-reload compose stacks plus CI and a VPS deploy workflow when asked.
finalize runs git init before bun install, because husky's prepare script needs .git to exist, then formats and makes the first commit.

decisions.title: Official scaffolders, not templates
decisions.body: App code always comes from upstream, so output matches whatever each framework ships today. Express is the one exception, because it has no official scaffolder.

decisions.title: Adapters only write inside their app
decisions.body: Adapters are declarative fragments, and root files belong to steps. Adding a framework means one adapter file and a registry entry, never a special case inside a step.

decisions.title: A red nightly is the system working
decisions.body: Scaffolders are version-pinned and the nightly matrix proves them on Ubuntu and Windows. A canary job strips the pins and runs against @latest, catching upstream changes before users do.

decisions.title: Built for coding agents too
decisions.body: In --json mode the only thing on stdout is one manifest, progress goes to stderr, and exit codes mean something: 0 ok, 1 step failed, 2 usage error.

deploy.comment: agent mode, with one JSON manifest on stdout
deploy.command: bun create bunship my-app --web next --api nest --docker --cicd --json

deploy.comment: release: pushing a tag publishes to npm with provenance

name: appctl
tagline: Makes the 101st deployment the same single command as the first.
summary: A port assigner and nginx server-block generator for a host-installed nginx fronting Docker apps, making the 101st deployment the same single command as the first.

It allocates a free host port from named tiers, writes and validates the nginx config, gets a Let's Encrypt certificate and reloads. If nginx -t ever fails, it rolls back cleanly. Containers publish on loopback only, so the internet can't bypass nginx even though Docker's iptables rules sidestep the firewall.

caseStudy.headline: The 101st deployment is the same command as the first.
problem: Fronting many Docker apps with one host nginx gets painful fast. For every project you pick a free port, edit compose, write a server block, symlink it, get a certificate and reload, all by hand and the same way every time.

One bad block in that routine can take nginx down for every app on the box. appctl turns it into a single command with one registry as the source of truth, and never reloads a config that hasn't passed nginx -t.

stackGroups.label: tls
stackGroups.items: certbot (Let's Encrypt) · shared origin cert · none

flow.title: What add does
flow.failState: test fails → roll back, running nginx untouched
steps: Pick a tier (prompted, or TIER=…) and take the first port in its band that is neither in the registry nor bound on the host.
Write an HTTP-only server block, enable it, test and reload, so certbot's http-01 challenge can be served.
Obtain the certificate with certbot certonly. If that fails, the working HTTP route stays up and appctl prints how to retry.
Rewrite the block with :443, the certbot hardening includes and an optional WebSocket upgrade, then test and reload again. If that test fails, it falls back to HTTP only.
Print the exact docker-compose ports line, bound to 127.0.0.1, to paste into the project.

decisions.title: The internet can't bypass nginx
decisions.body: Containers publish on 127.0.0.1. Docker's iptables rules bypass UFW and firewalld, so a 0.0.0.0 publish is exposed even behind a firewall deny rule.

decisions.title: A bad config never goes live
decisions.body: Every change runs nginx -t first. On failure appctl rolls back its own files and exits, leaving the running nginx and every other app untouched.

decisions.title: No certificate, no outage
decisions.body: The HTTP block goes live before certbot runs, so a DNS or port-80 problem leaves a working HTTP route instead of a half-written TLS block.

decisions.title: The registry decides
decisions.body: Every mapping lives in one TSV file. Rows change only after a successful test and reload, so a failure can never leave a dangling entry.

deploy.comment: deploy an app: port, nginx block, TLS, compose line
release: a pushed tag publishes the GitHub release

name: Ticketing App
tagline: Event ticketing as microservices on a NATS Streaming event bus, with common types and middleware published to npm.
summary: An event ticketing platform built as microservices, with a NATS Streaming event bus connecting independently deployable services.
It demonstrates event-driven architecture, asynchronous communication, and service isolation, with common types and middleware factored into a shared library published to npm.

diagram.title: Architecture: five services, one event bus

nodes.name: auth
nodes.detail: signup · signin · JWT cookie · own MongoDB

nodes.name: orders
nodes.detail: reserve with a 15-min window · own MongoDB

caseStudy.headline: Five services, one event bus, no shared database.
problem: A ticket can't be sold twice, an unpaid order has to release its ticket, and a payment has to complete exactly one order. All of that has to hold across services that never share a database.
The Ticketing App splits that into five independently deployable services that only talk through NATS Streaming events, each keeping its own MongoDB and its own copy of the data it needs.

flow.title: Buying a ticket
flow.failState: timer wins → order cancelled, ticket released
steps: Orders checks the ticket isn't already reserved, saves the order with a 15-minute expiry and publishes order:created.
Tickets reserves the ticket by setting its orderId and publishes ticket:updated, so every other copy stays in step.
Expiration queues a Bull job on Redis, delayed until the order expires.
Payments charges the card through a Stripe PaymentIntent and publishes payment:created, and Orders marks the order complete.
If the delayed job fires first, expiration:complete makes Orders cancel the order, and order:cancelled releases the ticket.

decisions.title: Services never call each other
decisions.body: Everything crosses NATS Streaming. Orders keeps its own replica of tickets, built from events, instead of asking the tickets service at request time.

decisions.title: Out-of-order events are rejected
decisions.body: Records carry a version through mongoose-update-if-current, and listeners only apply an event whose version is the next one, so a late message cannot overwrite newer data.

decisions.title: Scale out without double work
decisions.body: Each service subscribes with a queue group, so with several replicas running every event is still handled once.

decisions.title: One package for the protocol
decisions.body: Event subjects, payload types, base Listener and Publisher classes and auth middleware live in @robin_project/common on npm.

deploy.comment: build, deploy and watch every service

lessons: Saving a record and publishing its event aren't atomic yet, so a crash in between leaves other services out of sync. The fix is an outbox: write the event to the same database in one transaction and let a background worker publish it.
Orders validates ticketId as a MongoDB ObjectId, which quietly couples it to the tickets service's database. It should only check that the id is present and trust the replicated ticket data.

name: DevOps Capstone (AWS)
tagline: A VPC with public and private subnets: Terraform, Ansible, Docker, Prometheus + Grafana, and a Cloudflare Tunnel instead of public ingress.
summary: A capstone project provisioning an AWS VPC with public and private subnets end to end: Terraform for the infrastructure, Ansible for configuration, Docker for the workload.

Prometheus and Grafana handle monitoring, a Cloudflare Tunnel provides secure access without exposing public ingress, and GitHub Actions publishes the documentation site. The AWS resources have since been torn down.

nodes.name: GitHub Actions
nodes.detail: build image on push · docs to Pages

caseStudy.headline: Three servers, two subnets, zero clicks in the console.
problem: The bootcamp's final brief was to design, provision, configure, deploy, monitor and document a complete system, and to do it reproducibly instead of clicking around the AWS console.
Terraform builds the network and servers and writes the Ansible inventory. Ansible configures every box and runs the app from ECR. Prometheus and Grafana watch the web server from the private subnet.

flow.title: From nothing to monitored
steps: terraform apply builds the VPC, both subnets, the internet and NAT gateways, three Ubuntu servers and the ECR repository, with state kept in S3.
Terraform renders inventory.ini from a template with each server's IP, the SSH key and the ECR repository URI.
The playbook applies common to every host (AWS CLI, timezone, SSM agent), then docker and webapp to the web server, and docker and monitoring to the monitoring server.
The web server pulls the latest image from ECR and runs it on port 80.
Prometheus on the private monitoring server scrapes the web server at 10.0.0.5:9100, with Grafana on top.

decisions.title: Only the web server is public
decisions.body: The Ansible controller and the monitoring server live in the private subnet and reach the internet only outwards, through a NAT gateway.

decisions.title: The inventory is generated
decisions.body: Terraform renders the Ansible inventory from the resources it just created, so the playbook can never point at a stale IP.

decisions.title: Shell access through Session Manager
decisions.body: Every instance gets an SSM instance profile, so operators open a session through AWS rather than hopping through a jump host.

decisions.title: State lives in S3
decisions.body: Terraform state sits in an S3 backend instead of on one person's laptop.

deploy.comment: provision the network, servers and ECR (from terraform/)
configure every host and start the app (from ansible/)
